utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-00-39-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis, Nicola Piacente, and Julia Baly appear on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm attorney Goran Neskovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the gentleman with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Professor Radomir Lukic, legal expert for this preliminary motion hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The position is this: that, as you'll see, the Trial Chamber is not fully composed. Judge Bennouna is not able to be present this afternoon. We had hoped that by waiting he would be able to be present, but he cannot be. The position is this: that we are minded to adjourn this case until tomorrow afternoon in order that the Chamber could be fully composed to hear the arguments, but we recognise that that could cause inconvenience, and if it does, we'll hear counsel. The only alternative would be to address arguments to the Trial Chamber as it's presently composed, and then in due course we would give a ruling when we are fully composed. But it's a matter really for the parties to say how their convenience lies. As I say, we would normally suggest that the matter be adjourned until tomorrow afternoon in order that the Chamber could be fully composed then, but we are open to argument. Ms. Hollis, does the Prosecution have any submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection to either alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence also has no objection about the arguments being offered today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, which -- if I may put it to you like this: Would it be more convenient to you to put the arguments today to the two of us or would you rather wait and address the full Chamber tomorrow? It's a matter for which you would prefer, which is more convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is agreeable to submit arguments before the Trial Chamber as it is composed today. We have no objection on the third member of the Chamber being absent today, because the ruling, as we understand, is going to be given by the full Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear the arguments today and also deal with the Status Conference, which we can deal with. Mr. Neskovic, there are two matters we have to deal with. The first is the motion challenging jurisdiction. We have in respect of both the motions, of course, very full pleadings. The matter has been fully argued and the oral submissions really should be restricted to deal with any matters which are not covered in the written pleadings. And of course, in respect of this particular motion, the fact is that the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has ruled on the matter and we are bound by their rulings, unless there is some significant reason. Well, the Appeals Chamber can -- should take a different view about it. But as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we are bound by what they say. Now, what would you like to add to your written submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence, including Mr. Lukic, expert for international law, has prepared a lengthier document. Obviously there are some repetitions, but there are some new arguments included which we can present separately so that we avoid reading the entire document, but just the new portions which we had not submitted already in our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps you would like to summarise the new arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With your permission, Mr. President, before starting the presentation of new arguments of the Defence, I would just like to add a comment passed on by Mr. Krajisnik that be assisted not only by the counsel but also by the pro bono legal experts. The ruling on the 14th of July, the Defence is aware of the ruling and does not want to object to it. But pursuant to Article 16 of the Statute and Rule 45 of the Rules, the experts who are supposed to represent the accused would be representing him pro bono rather than at the expense of Tribunal. Also, we would like to point out that the existing practice of the Tribunal, where the same counsel appears in various positions in various trials, such as Celebici, Nikolic, and Brdjanin, to cite but one example. However, we will not appeal this ruling. Your Honours, first of all, I would like to point out that the Defence, in its preliminary motions and in their responses to the Prosecutor's replies, we have presented our arguments but will now just present the new arguments and only comment very briefly on the ones previously stated. As regards the jurisdiction of ICTY, I would expressly ask the Trial Chamber that Mr. Lukic present the arguments, because it is the position of the Defence that it would be done in a much more economic way. And I have to point out that the Prosecution did not oppose the presence of the expert's submission today, but only pointed out the reservation that only one counsel address one issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As just agreed, I will present some new arguments relating to the issue of command responsibility from Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. With respect to everything else contained in our motion previously submitted and which relates to the legality of this and legitimacy of this Tribunal -- [Technical difficulty] -- relating the legitimacy and legality of this Tribunal, the Defence abides by the position taken previously. By presenting new arguments which relate to Article 7(3) of the Statute, that is, the issue of command responsibility, the position of the Defence is that the command responsibility does not have the status, that is, that it is not an international custom. The first case of command responsibility is the case of Jamarsta, is a very dubious precedent. Prior to that case, there was no legal practice regarding this type of responsibility which could be taken as a model by the commission which had convicted this general. The commission was composed of officers but not of qualified legal experts. The very development of the rules on which the Yamashita decision is based was based on an analogy on certain statutes of the US legal system. All these statutes without exception were not part of criminal but rather other branches of law. A specific case, the case in question was conducted on the basis of comments and positions taken by General McArthur, one of the Defence lawyers for General Yamashita. He argues this point in his book, "The Case of General Yamashita." Due to judicial economy and rational expenditure of our time, we will not go into all deficiencies of this trial which was concluded in 1943, but the Defence raises the question of whether such a case, which is full of legal shortcomings, whether such a case will build a model for our future cases. Other cases relative to this matter were the Nuremberg trials. The judges had an easier job of establishing the case using the precedent of Yamashita. Regardless of the shortcomings of the Yamashita case, the Nuremberg judges still relied on it. In the case of the German supreme command, the Judges pointed to the significant changes in the structure of supreme command, and in the second case, the question of hostages, the Yamashita case was also used as a precedent. The case against General Toyoda was completed in 1949 and that is the last case before now dealing with the doctrine of command responsibility. After the completion of all trials against war crimes committed during World War II, the United Nations undertook the codification of laws developed during these trials. The convention on the Prosecution of crimes against genocide was adopted in 1948 and did not include the command responsibility. The Geneva Conventions, adopted by the auspices of the International Red Cross in 1949, also do not recognise command responsibility even though they contain a number of prohibitive and normative rules. The main result of those efforts is the code of crimes against humanity which was adopted by the United Nations in 1954. This code also did not include command responsibility. The question then arises, if, as is alleged by the Prosecution, command responsibility has become the case, why a document of such significance never provided for it. The US manual, field manual of 27.10 issued by the US military institutions does provide for command responsibility, but omits the concept of military justice. The question arises how is it then possible that a manual of the ground forces of one of the branches of the US army recognises it but not such a lot [as interpreted] institutions. We believe that the judge who issued the instructions to the jury in the case of Captain Medina between 1971 and 1975 which dealt with the issue of command responsibility completely failed to point to the manual 27.10. We therefore ask: How is it possible that the judge is in contravention of this military manual and is contrary to the international customary law? Our answer is as follows: There is no command responsibility as an international custom because the judge in this case would have recognised it and followed it, and as far as the provisions of the field manual is concerned, the judge violated them because they are in opposition to the common law provisions of criminal responsibility. Your Honours, in the other two cases in which the issue of command responsibility was dealt, there was no legal -- no indictments were issued. The superior of Captain Medina was questioned by the court and General Kostera was questioned, but no trial was ever conducted against him only disciplined in 1971. The next case is the case of General Vestmorlenda who was the chief commander in Vietnam. This case never reached the courts, even though there were indicia that there were elements of his command responsibility involved. However, the national security advisor disallowed the trial and instead, ordered an investigation which acquitted General Vestmorlenda. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In 1977, additional protocols to the Geneva Conventions were adopted and for the first time in history, they codified the command responsibility. However, the additional protocols all mention the disciplinary and criminal responsibility based on the omission to act but only in a case to case basis. The Christian -- members of a Christian phalanx in Lebanon burst into the camps in southern Chatila and carried out a massacre of refugees and they were under the orders of the -- under the control of the Israeli forces. The Cahan Commission investigated the case and ordered that several generals be disciplined, but no criminal proceedings were ever initiated against these soldiers. In 1995, the Canadian command of forces which were stationed in Somalia were also faced with a case when the local population was looking for food and some crimes were committed as a result of it. The unit was pulled from the duty in Somalia and we have no end results of this investigation. There was an investigating commission which determined that the Minister of Defence in collusion with some other public officials tried to silence the whole case. This was followed by the resignations first of the Minister, and then the Chief of General Staff. Both of them implicitly recognising their responsibility for it. After the Toyoda case, the first next case dealing with the command responsibility were -- are the cases of Delalic and Kvocka, both before this Tribunal. The judgements in either of these cases are still not final. If we assume that they will become final in the course of this year, it would mean that 51 years had elapsed since the last case of command responsibility was judged, that is against General Toyoda in 1951. If we take into account the generally-held view that the customary law presupposes the awareness of the legal force of such a law, the Defence questions how it is possible that something is perceived as customary if it had not been practised for over half a century. The command responsibility started in 19 -- was created in 1946 and it was used until 1949 in cases which have often been described as the justice of the victors. If this command responsibility statute was only practised for three years, and that it established an international norm, the question arises whether this practice, in these 51 years of non-practice, is still valid as custom even if at one point it was considered a custom. All cases of omission to act which took place between 1949 and 2000 have ended with disciplinary or political consequences. The additional protocols of Geneva Conventions is the only document which recognises command responsibility for omissions to act and it is this only document that is in existence. It defines these command responsibilities, either criminal or disciplinary, based on the case. Since this statute has not been practised for 51 years and the disciplinary and the political responsibility have been practised, the Defence submits that the command responsibility does exist as an international custom, but only as a disciplinary statute. Even if there was an international practice which implied criminal responsibility and criminal sanctions, and we are referring to the period between 1946 and 1949, this statute has certainly become obsolete by now and it has also changed. Mr. President, these are the new arguments relative to the status of command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, in your historical review --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I have some problems.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Professor, that in your historical review, you didn't mention the Rome Statute establishing the International Criminal Court, perhaps because it has not yet entered into force. But it is a very significant instrument, having been signed by well over one hundred countries. That also establishes and reflects command responsibility. Would you say that when the Rome Statute addressed the concept of command responsibility that that was a new concept, that that was new law?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my historical survey of the evolution of command responsibility, we did not consider the Rome Statute and the new permanent International Criminal Court, because it goes beyond the time frame covered by the indictment of our client. Because all that we said concerns the violation of the fundamental principle of criminal law, nullum crimen sine lege, nullum penae sine lege. The Rome Statute appeared years after the period of time when it is alleged that our client committed certain criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Professor. But of course, although it appears after the time of the commission of the offence, if what is in the Rome Statute reflects customary international law, then that would not matter if the custom had emerged prior to the commission of the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our concept is, as you have seen, that this question could not be considered as an international custom because it does not meet the basic conditions for a particular behaviour to set up -- to become a practice that will then become the source of international law. And on the basis of your question and my answer, I think that the Rome Statute is written law, is the law of treaties, and it is something quite different from what we are claiming, and that, in point of fact, it is a novel approach and a novel concept as against the previous period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, if you want to reply, perhaps briefly, to anything said today, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that our written reply covers these new arguments. We have nothing further to add on that, unless Your Honours have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you. We turn now to the second motion. This is a motion on the part of the Defence alleging defects in the form of the indictment. Mr. Neskovic, we have your submissions again and a response from the Prosecution and your further submissions. It must be said that a great deal of the matter you raise really relates either to matters of evidence, because you'll appreciate there's a distinction between what is in the indictment and what is a matter properly covered by evidence or by matters which are really not matters of detail which the Prosecution should be required to go into in relation to an indictment. However, you do, at the latter part of your motion, ask for clarification of the criminal responsibility alleged against your client, relying on the decision, in particular, of this Trial Chamber -- it's open to you to rely on it -- in Dosen and Kolundzija. Now, those are the matters you cover. If there's anything new you want to add, then of course you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have already answered. I was about to, once again, point out the Dosen and Kolundzija annex regarding the form of the indictment, because when we analysed the response to the Defence's motion, we noticed, amongst other things, that the Prosecutor points out that the political officials in the indictment, their alleged individual responsibility needs not to be defined in relation to -- pursuant to Article 7(1) and (3), as it is described, allegedly, for so-called direct perpetrators of acts. This position we find rather strange, so the Defence asks whether different rules apply to political officials in the doctrine of criminal law. Are the political officials, because they are engaged in politics, proclaimed guilty in advance? The Tribunal should not allow the Prosecutor to file indictments on political grounds. Indictments are acts and law, and therefore they must abide by legal norms. The Prosecutor claims that my client, Mr. Krajisnik, is guilty because he was the President of the parliament of Republika Srpska, because, according to the Prosecutor, the Assembly of Republika Srpska is also a form of a criminal organisation, and likewise, Mr. Krajisnik is, by extension, a criminal, even though the Defence is aware that a large number of allegations in the indictment is a matter for the trial to be resolved. Nevertheless, the Defence should like to point out the latest Tribunal's practice in the case against Krnojelac. In that case, the Chamber ruled that the Prosecutor should rephrase the indictment in the spirit of the principles which govern all the legal systems; that is, in cases when the Prosecutor alleges that somebody is guilty because he belonged to an alleged criminal organisation, then their participation, their membership, must be proven beyond any reasonable doubt. Therefore, if the Prosecutor alleges in the indictment that my client, because he was a member of the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, and because he was the president of the lawfully elected parliament, that he is, because of that, therefore responsible, allegedly, for illegal acts, then it must be brought into harmony with legal standards applicable to the indictments. However, the Prosecutor omitted to inform the accused with the details of his alleged criminal responsibility deriving from his office or the specific political institution. In other words, if the accused is to enjoy his right and prepare his Defence properly, then the Prosecutor must, beyond any reasonable doubt, specify the criminal responsibility of the accused. The Prosecutor has omitted to do that, and the Defence believes that the Chamber should inform the Prosecution that the same legal standard should be applied to political officials as to all other individuals. On the basis of the above said, in our written motions and in our response, and today the Defence once again respectfully submits that in this case the standard be applied -- the standard introduced by both this Chamber and other Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, such as, for instance, in the decisions on preliminary motions in Dosen and Kolundzija case, and that the Prosecution be ordered to prepare an annex that would make part -- an integral part of the indictment so as to specify there the following. I do not want to repeat all that, Your Honours, because we already pointed it out in our first preliminary motion. It has to do with, the first column, the exact form of participation, instigation, issuance of orders, and so on and so forth; and the second one, the precise time frame and locality for the criminal acts; the third is classification of criminal offences pursuant to our Tribunal Statute; and the fourth column, precise form of individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) and 7(3), or both of them. The Defence believes that such an approach of the Prosecution would contribute to removing most of the vague points in the indictment and that such an amended indictment would meet the standards in Article 18(4) of the Tribunal Statute and Rule 47(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Evidence. I should also like to touch upon, with Your Honour's leave: In paragraph 78 of the answer to the preliminary response to the preliminary form of the indictment, the Prosecution says, and I am quoting: "As to the accused's complaint regarding use of the concept of A Greater Serbia, it is an appropriate characterisation which is consistent with the Prosecution's theory of this case." The indictment is basically the position of one party to the case that allegedly describes and the liability on the part of the accused, and thus needs not be impartial. Certainly the use of the term in the indictment is not inflammatory or unreasonable. The Prosecution therefore denies that it has attempted to mislead. However, the rub of the problem is that the Prosecution ascribes the concept of Greater Serbia a completely wrong meaning, that is, a criminal concept in itself which automatically presumes ethnic cleansing, ethnic persecution, and so on and so forth. Even though repeatedly in the response to the motion regarding the former indictment, the Prosecution defends its right to arbitrariness and generalities, claiming that it is not bound to explain the meaning of individual terms that it uses in the indictment, that it is not bound to explain its concept and the like. The Defence considers that the Prosecution has simply gone too far, because it requests the alleged right to misuse, that is, complete distortion of the true meaning of a term. For instance, "the Greater Serbia," the Prosecution does not treat this term within its historical concept in which that term emerged but views it from some different point of view or within the context of different impression and propaganda. For instance, Professor Gart, on 28th of June, 1996, in a case before this Tribunal, IT-95-T-61 -- this is the case of the Prosecutor versus Karadzic and Mladic. I believe it is page 38 of the French version. It says: "The notion of the Greater Serbia does not explicitly mean ethnic cleansing." However, on the basis of what happened in Croatia, one can see that it also meant that. With all due respect, even Professor Gart makes a mistake, and a double one. What happened in Croatia, that is, military operations of the Croatian army, called Tempest and Storm, definitively refute Professor Gart. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'm going to interrupt you. These are really matters for argument and evidence. They're not matters for the -- for an indictment or for argument about an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was about to say that the Defence thought that this was a matter for the trial, but that it is because of such thesis' that the indictment has a slanted view. I have nothing else to add regarding the form of the indictment, and I should like to suggest, with your leave, to take due note of the arguments of the Defence and to order the Prosecution to prepare the annex and amended indictment, as specified in our motion and our response -- and the Defence's response to the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, the argument being put forward in relation to clarification is that what appears in the indictment from time to time -- and one can see it, for instance, in paragraph 10 -- is a very generalised allegation which essentially repeats the words of the Statute. For instance: "That the accused, acting individually or in concert with others, planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation, or execution of the destruction, in whole or in part, of the religious group." Now, is there any reason why you shouldn't specify what it is that you say this accused did in terms of planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or otherwise aiding and abetting? What is it that you allege that he did? And necessarily, therefore, what is the case that he has got to meet? Now, is there any reason why that shouldn't be set out at this stage in an indictment, or, as we did in Dosen and Kolundzija, order an annex to be attached to the indictment, setting out -- the case I think you were in -- setting out the nature of the allegations in the form of participation? Is there any distinction between that case and this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the modes of liability that are set out in Article 7(1) are, in fact, legal characterisations of conduct and what we set forward in the indictment is conduct. It is for the fact-finder to determine the legal characterisations of that conduct so that we would not elect between the modes of liability. That's the reason that we don't elect between the modes of liability. In terms of setting out the conduct, we suggest that we have set it out with sufficient particularity in this indictment insofar as we have indicated in this indictment that we are dealing with the very highest level of accused whose participation was at the very highest level. The conduct of this accused is set out throughout this indictment in various paragraphs. Basically that conduct being his participation in various organisations or bodies which, themselves, had direction and control over other bodies and organisations and entities which led to the commission of these crimes. We have indicated what bodies and organisations and entities we allege he was a member of that led to this liability. We have indicated that he was one of the leading members of the SDS and that he and Karadzic, in particular, were the two leading policy members -- policy makers of the SDS, and that it was the SDS that created this concept of this Greater Serbia or at least revitalised it. And it was his participation this in the SDS including the main board that the structures were set up that were the means by which these crimes were committed were the vehicles, if you will, through which these crimes were committed. That also, he was a member of the Presidency and a member of the National Security Council and in that capacity more directly, perhaps, than through the SDS, in that capacity, he had control over Bosnian Serb forces which we have defined. He also had control over the SDS and government authorities who were the ones who, as we go down the layers of control and direction, ultimately are the ones who, if you will, in quotation marks, "committed the crimes" that are charged in this indictment. If we look at some of the paragraphs that speak about this in terms of the SDS, his membership and the functions of the SDS in this overall plan of ethnic cleansing which is the plan that we set forward in the indictment. If you look at paragraph two, it indicates his membership on the main board. If you look at paragraph 12, paragraph 24, paragraph 28, paragraph 41, paragraph 42, paragraph 45, paragraph 46, paragraph 47, 48, 49, they set out the various functions of the main board. They set out the involvement of the SDS of which we say he was in control in the crimes that were committed. If we look at the control over the Bosnian Serb forces through the Presidency and through the National Security Council, if we look at paragraphs 7, paragraph 8, paragraph 14, 16, 20, 27, 47, those paragraphs also make reference to the way in which this entity was involved in the crimes that were committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina within the time period alleged, and also his membership in the various parts of these organisations. We believe, in terms of his conduct, we have set that forward in the indictment itself. In terms of looking at his membership in the Bosnian assembly, if we look at paragraphs 29, 48 and 54, we talk about his membership there and we also indicated in the indictment the kinds of actions that were carried out through this assembly of which he was the president, in our view, as the president was able to be a leader and director of what happened. So in terms of conduct, we believe that we have set it out in various paragraphs throughout the indictment and that that is sufficient to put this person on notice of what it is he needs to defend against. In terms of the second question, Your Honour, and that has to do with setting out a schedule, we would suggest, Your Honours that there is a very critical difference between this case and cases at the level of Kolundzija or Dosen who were shift leaders in one camp, in one opstina during a certain period of time. Our theory is quite simple. For this accused, he was in charge of everything that happened in that country during the time period alleged because of his participation in these various organs, because of his association with other members of these organs, these bodies, these entities. So we do not need the particularity that we would need with a low-level offender. We look, instead, at categories of his involvement, at categories of offences of which he is guilty, at categories of victims, at categories of perpetrators. When it comes to the time frames alleged, we have put those in the indictment. We also put the places in the indictment. And we believe when you look at proximity to the people who were actually torturing, beating, killing and carrying out the operations in the camps and detention facilities, when we look at his proximity to that, it is far enough removed that it is the categories which are the most instructive because it is the categories of the offenders which make him liable. They must fall within the Bosnian Serb forces or the members of the SDS or the government authorities. But as to which individual it is, the only relevance the individual has is whether they fall within those categories. So that we suggest that indeed for this level of offender, we have provided sufficient particularity and that a schedule would, in fact, be our proof of his culpability, would not be an indictment, material facts, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, is there anything you'd like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor more or less repeats the argument she gave in her response to our motion and we -- and the Defence disagrees with them. I should like to add two things. First, in paragraph 22, the accused is charged that he had control over SDS boards and Crisis Staffs. However, it needs to be said that the SDS was the Serb political party. Nobody has so far, not even some body of the International Community has proclaimed the SDS a criminal organisation or its activities as criminal activities. As for the never-failing invariable linkage, association of the accused with Dragan Karadzic, we need to say that in paragraph 22 in -- about the rulings on the motions in Kvocka case, the Chamber took over certain paragraphs from the Krnojelac decision and decided that the Prosecution could not name those who were participating directly in those crimes, but that it would suffice to indicate that category and their position as a group. The Defence believes that the same thing should be done in this case too, because in paragraph 30 of the answer, the Prosecutor has already reduced the term with others and said "with other leaders. " So the Prosecution has thus shown that it is possible to be more specific. And as for the paragraph 5, that he was engaged in these activities alone or with -- together with Dragan Karadzic, evidently the Prosecution only intends to emphasise the activity of the accused alleging that he was a close associate of Dragan Karadzic. The Defence does not know because the history of the criminal law does not know of the case that the criminal activity on somebody is being proven by his association of a person who has not been pronounced guilty or brought to trial. We, therefore, do not think that this paragraph has any legal grounds and, again, we believe that the Prosecution should attach an annex to the indictment because whatever the case, the Defence -- it would be easier for the Defence to prepare the Defence if there is such attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider these matters and give our rulings on both motions in due course. I turn next to the Status Conference which is to follow the Motions Hearing, and the purpose of that is to review the position as far as the case is concerned and also as the Rule provides to review the conditions of detention. We will begin by reviewing the position as far as the case is concerned and perhaps, Ms. Hollis, you can assist us with how far things have got.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, we are in the process of building binders for the witnesses that have been identified to date through the confirmation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. materials so that we can complete our disclosure as to those witnesses. We are also in the process, which will be a somewhat lengthy process, of reviewing and collating the documentary evidence in this case that may be of relevance in this case and may be subject to disclosure under the various rules of the Tribunal. As we find that evidence and review it, we are also putting that also into categories so we can determine what we will disclose. We note in that regard that it's interesting that the Rules require that witness statements be disclosed, that the -- any statements of the accused be disclosed, but when it comes to documentary evidence that are not in the form of witness statements, we are to provide a list but not by the Rules, themselves, on our own to provide disclosure of those documents. The Prosecution will be reviewing its position in that regard with a view to expediting the trial because we believe that quite a few documents will be of relevance. And we will, to the extent we believe we can do so, will provide the documents themselves in advance as part of our disclosure even though the Rules, themselves, do not exactly require that. But we believe it would unduly delay the trial proceeding if we were not to act in that way. We have provided some additional documentary disclosure to the Defence. Since counsel have been very gracious with us in notifying us of what materials he has not received or has not been in legible form among the receipts that we have provided to him, and we are undertaking to provide him with material that either was inadvertently not provided or to giving him a second copy in case somehow it was mislaid in translation. So we are proceeding with disclosure in that regard. We are also, in our own case, reviewing additional witnesses that may be needed for the case. Of course, as Your Honours are aware, we have a very large crime base and witnesses who are directly relevant to the crime base will constitute a large part of our case. In addition to that, however, there are witnesses who could perhaps expedite the case by providing some sort of summary or overview evidence. We are reviewing that possibility. We may also feel the need to call upon experts and international personnel who may have had contact with this accused or others in areas of discussion that are relevant to this case. So we are reviewing the needs for those witnesses, and we are attempting to go line up interviews with those so that we can disclose statements of those witnesses as well. So we are, at this point in time, Your Honours, organising the case in a way that will facilitate both our preparation for the case and will facilitate comprehensive disclosure to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the witnesses are concerned, when do you anticipate finalising disclosure of the relevant statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We don't think that we will be able to do that much before the end of this year, the beginning of next year, given the fact that some of the people we need to interview are very difficult to get on their schedules. But we hope that we will be able to provide a large amount of the crime base disclosure by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you shouldn't disclose, as early as possible, the material which you do have which you know you're going to rely on?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And any additional material when you have it at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's what we're attempting to do, Your Honour, that as we accumulate it, as we review it, we will disclose it so that it will be a continuing process and the Defence will not be in the position of receiving hundreds of pages at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the documents are concerned, I understand the process you are undertaking. It will certainly be of assistance to the Trial Chamber if only those documents which are really relevant are relied on as opposed to putting in anything which might possibly be relevant. It is a very useful exercise for the Prosecution at the outset, if I may say, to identify those documents on which they are really going to rely rather than having a flood of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that is really the goal of this comprehensive search that we're doing now so that we can be sure that we have identified all of the documents that will be of most assistance to the Trial Chamber in the presentation of our case, and certainly this is a very large case, as Your Honours are aware. Having said that, we certainly do agree that we must take it upon ourselves to make the best use of the fewest number of documents and witnesses that we can possibly use and still prove our case. So we're looking at that approach as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the end of the year for the documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the documents will be longer than the end of the year because of the hundreds of thousands of pages that we're looking at in terms of searches. We are putting in place a very comprehensive programme to do that which will involve a large number of additional personnel and hardware and software. So we will not be in a position to say we have completed our search and review of the documents by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are, of course, problems about getting cases on here, but if it's right that you're not going to be ready for trial by the end of the year, when are you going to be ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that we will be ready to proceed to trial June or July of next summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a year's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think you should look at that again. I don't know what the position is going to be, of course, about court availability, but as far as the Prosecution are concerned, it will mean that this accused would have been in custody for 14 months before the Prosecution will be ready for trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And Your Honour, we believe, given the complexity of this case, the amount of evidence involved, that that would not be an unduly long length of time. And should Your Honours wish any sort of written submission on that, we're prepared to do so, but we believe that that would be -- that would not be a violation of a speedy trial. We will look at it again. We have been looking at it for the last several months as we have been looking at our resources, our other commitments, what is needed for this. And so the time frame that I am giving you is already a considered time frame, but we certainly will review that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, as a matter of principle, 14 months can't be considered a reasonable and acceptable time frame for preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest that it can, in that, indeed, in the international case law, there is support for that and we believe that it would be a reasonable period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are under the scrutiny of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is a reasonable time frame, it has certain implications, of which account will have to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We are aware of the some of the implications that you may be considering, Your Honour, and we are prepared to address those with that in written form as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give us some idea at this stage of the scope of the trial that you envisage.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And at this stage, Your Honour, we are speaking from the standpoint of having to fully litigate these issues, because other than, perhaps, an armed conflict existed, there is no stipulation or admission at this point, and that we are going to have to fully litigate it in terms of the crime base with eyewitnesses. We're looking at approximately 42 municipalities involved in a pattern of criminal activity. We're also looking at specific alleged camps and specific alleged killings, and we believe, in order to bring forward even the crime base with no overlap on our witnesses, we're looking at a minimum of four witnesses per municipality, and so we're looking at something like 160 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. We have some experience in this. The way in which it can be approached, I suggest, is in this way, and which you might like to think about, is that: For each of these municipalities or camps or alleged offences, you think in terms of calling a witness, your best witness, and putting that witness on and seeing what the cross-examination, if any, is. And in that way, it may be that you can reduce drastically the number of witnesses. It may be necessary to call more; it may not be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in coming up with that number per municipality, that was the approach we had planned to take. Some of the things that we can do to expedite the trial -- there's really nothing we can do on our own to expedite it. We can propose various modes of presentation of evidence, but the Trial Chamber must accept those. For example, certainly we can use affidavits where we can get a suitable document from certain countries, but that's corroboration only. We can look at the use of prior testimony or prior statements as part, at least, or perhaps all of direct examination, but that depends on whether the Trial Chamber will allow. Judicial notice is a possibility to speed up things, but that is whether the Court will take judicial notice. If the Trial Chamber were to find, as a matter of law, certain jurisdictional elements at the beginning of the trial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- that's within the province of the Trial Chamber after hearing the Defence's position. Stipulations and admissions also, but that depends on the Defence. So we are looking at those sorts of things, but we feel it's incumbent upon us at this point in time, even using a minimalist approach of witnesses, to put Your Honours on notice of what we feel should be necessary should none of those things be available to us. So that, if you will, we have before you our estimate of what it would take if none of those shortcuts are available, so that there is no surprise later if, in fact, that is what it takes. But we are looking at the kinds of things you have mentioned, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say four witnesses for the 42 municipalities each. How many other witnesses have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are also looking at the possibility of using overview witnesses or summary witnesses, expert witnesses. We're looking at the need, perhaps, for expert witnesses regarding the political spectrum, SDS, the Assembly, perhaps, to put on expert evidence about that. Also expert evidence relating to the military, the Main Staff, the chain of command, how it relates to the Presidency, to the National Security Council, how information and orders and directives flow up and down. We also, of course, are looking at the possibility of expert evidence for police, and we are looking at the possibility of expert evidence in the area of demographics, given the fact that we do have genocide as a charge. And we're looking, as I said earlier, as witnesses who, through their various associations and international bodies, such as UNPROFOR or other organisations, would have evidence relevant to this proceeding regarding both the accused's direct participation and their involvement with bodies at meetings where perhaps he was not present but he was a member of that body collectively. So given that, we're looking at as many as perhaps 50 or 60 of those witnesses. And again, this is an estimate now, without us being able to have completed our interviews. We don't wish to have a longer trial than is necessary; however, we are very cognizant of our requirement to prove our case beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So giving the best estimate that you can at the moment, how long do you anticipate the Prosecution case will take?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, if we look at a fully litigated case, maximising witness testimony, including crime base or eyewitnesses to these crimes, we believe that our case would take over a year. And that's assuming that we would have five days a week of being able to put on evidence five to six hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, clearly you will be having in mind, as you've said, the drafting of admissions or stipulations to see whether matters can be expedited in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We clearly will have to return to this whole matter Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. within not too long a distance and have another conference in order to see how we can expedite this trial. Are there any other matters you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I find myself the bearer of news that Your Honours don't want to hear on many occasions, but I believe it's important for us to put forward for you our recent assessment of what it takes, and we have no further matters at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, at this stage there is really little that you can assist us about, but we'll hear, of course, any submissions you want to make. It may be of assistance if, once the Prosecution have drafted any possible admissions or stipulations, as they're called in some jurisdictions, whether there aren't matters which can be agreed between the parties, matters of background and that sort of thing, which would shorten the trial and would certainly shorten the time necessary getting to trial. But at this stage it's too early, of course, for anything like that to have been arranged. Now, is there anything you would like to raise? We'll deal with the conditions of detention in due course, but this is merely to review the progress of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, I have nothing special to add except to confirm that the Defence counsel has been meeting with the Prosecutor's side and that we were provided a binder of material which is peripheral, really, and we would urge the Prosecution to speed up the process so that we could start preparing. On the other hand, we have initiated our process of gathering material. And as far as the conditions of detention are concerned, we will definitely file a motion for provisional release, but that will come in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to go into -- unless there's anything more you want to say about the case, I propose to go into private session to deal with any matters concerning the conditions of detention. But is there anything further you want to raise about the case or the progress of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For now, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think before we go into private session we should fix a date for the next Status Conference, which I will do with the assistance of the legal officer, saying that it should be sooner rather than later, given what we've heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm told that a suitable date would be available on the 27th of September, during the afternoon. I think that is a time for us to review again the progress of this case. Two months will have elapsed, and I hope that some progress will have been made, which we can then deal with. If there are no other matters to be dealt with in open session, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Conference adjourned at 5.56 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Motion Hearing and Status
